Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

I can't stop bad things from happening to me
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: 'Listening for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home' implies a home-intrusion/assault threat script. For a terrorism trauma in a combat pilot, this is not impossible, but it is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile because no other items indicate a home-invasion-type trauma context.

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: 'I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is more typically linked to sexual assault or interpersonal violation. In this profile it does not fit well with terrorism trauma and is not supported by the other selected triggers, threat, or strategy items.

issues.item: Male Presence: Being alone with men
issues.explanation: 'Being alone with men' as a trigger suggests an interpersonal male-perpetrator association. That conflicts with the stated terrorism trauma unless there was an additional gendered assault component, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Claire Donnelly is a 45-year-old combat pilot who came to treatment after months of telling herself she should be able to handle this on her own. The event she returns to began during a stateside security deployment when a terrorist bombing struck the military airfield where she was preparing for a flight. She remembers the blast first as sound and pressure—a violent bang that seemed to split the air, followed by alarms, shouting, and the crush of people forcing themselves through a narrow interior corridor toward the exit. In the surge she was pinned shoulder to shoulder with others, unable to move freely, breathing in dust and the sharp chemical smell of smoke. For a few moments she felt trapped, physically unwell, and certain that another explosion might come before she could get out. That combination of loud noise, crowding, confinement, and the sickened feeling in her body has remained fixed as the emotional core of the event.

In the weeks afterward, those same sensations quickly became charged. On base, the slam of a hangar door or the sudden thunder of engines could make Claire stiffen as if her body had already decided she was back in danger. A packed briefing room or a congested terminal was enough to make her scan for exits and think, with mounting certainty, that the world was simply dangerous and that safety could vanish without warning. When she felt even slightly nauseated, overheated, or short of breath, what frightened her most was not just the discomfort itself but what it seemed to prove: that she could not deal with even a small upset, that her body would fail her when she needed it, that bad things happened before she had any chance to stop them.

Those conclusions hardened over time. Claire had come to believe that she was less capable than she used to be and strangely defenseless despite a career built on composure under pressure. She often told herself that it could have been worse, that other people died and she did not, but this comparison brought only brief relief before the same bleak beliefs returned. Because she felt helpless in the face of danger and doubted her ability to manage distress, she began structuring her life around escape and control. She started avoiding enclosed spaces whenever she could, taking stairs instead of elevators, standing near doors in meetings, and delaying her presence in small packed rooms until the last possible minute. She also smoked more regularly, stepping outside between tasks for cigarettes in a way she described as the only thing that reliably brought her down fast enough to function.

These habits began to shape her days as much as the memories did. At work on the airfield, Claire now positions herself at the edge of the ready room and leaves if it becomes too crowded, which has made her seem abrupt and less available to junior crew. If she feels physically off—lightheaded, congested, vaguely sick—she is more likely to smoke and stay outdoors, and the open air feels safer precisely because it is not enclosed. Yet this way of coping keeps the original danger vivid for her. The more she organizes herself around avoiding tight spaces and relying on cigarettes to settle her body, the more quickly crowds, loud noises, and ordinary spells of feeling unwell register as signs that something is wrong again.

Her sense of threat is now nearly constant. Claire sleeps poorly, waking often and lying alert to every sound in her apartment building. In parking lots and on sidewalks she repeatedly checks behind her, as if someone may be approaching unnoticed. That constant watchfulness leaves her exhausted, and in that exhausted state she feels even less able to cope, more convinced that the world is dangerous and that she cannot prevent harm if it comes. Being so on guard also makes the environment feel full of triggers: a crowded grocery store becomes intolerable, a car backfiring feels instantly menacing, a spell of fatigue or nausea is interpreted as the beginning of losing control.

Her attempts to manage that alarm intensify it. Smoking gives her a few minutes of relief, but she notices afterward that she remains keyed up, still listening for sounds and still checking over her shoulder. Avoiding enclosed places means she rarely stays long enough anywhere to learn that the danger does not escalate, so each return to a cramped elevator, a packed operations room, or even a busy bar feels as potent as the last. She has become increasingly certain that if she lets down her guard or finds herself trapped again, she will not be able to handle what happens next.

Claire finally sought help after leaving a mandatory personnel briefing when the room filled beyond capacity and someone dropped a metal case behind her with a sharp crack. She was outside smoking within seconds, shaken by how fast she had bolted and by the realization that her life had narrowed around exits, cigarettes, and vigilance. She says she wants her discipline back, but beneath that is a more private hope: to stop feeling that danger is everywhere and to find out whether she can still trust herself when her body and the world both seem suddenly unsafe.
